Keywords: ”precursor” radiation, multiple scale analysis, fast-slow decomposition

Multiple-scale analysis on the radiation within the nonlinearly coupled KdV equations

Journal: Nonlinearity
Yezheng Li Email: yezheng@sas.upenn.edu    Joseph A. Biello Email: biello@math.ucdavis.edu    Yerong Li Email: yerong.li@caltech.edu Affiliation:  Department of Applied Physics and Materials Science, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, CA 91125, USA
Abstract

A multiple scale model of the nonlinearly coupled KdV equations is established to predict mechanism of interaction of equatorial Rossby waves and barotropic waves in certain case. Analytically, predicted precursor radiation is a centrosymmetric object and is shown in excellent quantitative agreement with numerical simulations; furthermore, the multiple scale model elucidates the salient mechanisms of the interaction of solitary waves and the mechanism for radiation. While the atmosphere-ocean science community is very interested in theoretical studies of tropical wave interactions and in developing reduced dynamical models that can explain some key features of equatorial phenomena, our analytic predictions quantitively explain formation of radiation during interaction in Biello’s model beyond qualitative level.

1 Introduction

1.1 Atmospheric background and solitary structures

Some poorly understood phenomena in atmosphere-ocean science involve a complex nonlinear interaction of clouds, moisture, and convection on a large variety of scales in both time and space, ranging from cumulus clouds over a few kilometers to intraseasonal oscillations over planetary scales of order 40,000 km [1, 2, 3, 4]. While current numerical simulations still fail to capture mechanism of interaction on multiple scales [1, 3, 5], ocean-atmosphere science community is interested in theoretical studies of tropical wave interactions and in developing reduced dynamical models that can at least qualitatively explain some key features of equatorial phenomena [6, 1, 2, 7, 3, 5, 8, 9].

Under this circumstance, amptitude equations describing the interaction of equatorial Rossby waves and barotropic waves

at−(1−2​γ)​ax​x​x+(a​b)x\displaystyle a_{t}-(1-2\gamma)a_{xxx}+(ab)_{x} =0,\displaystyle=0, (1)
bt−bx​x​x+(a22)x\displaystyle b_{t}-b_{xxx}+\left(\frac{a^{2}}{2}\right)_{x} =0,\displaystyle=0, (2)

are derived by Biello and Majda [6, 7] and are used as a model for long range interactions (teleconnections) between the tropical and midlatitude troposphere. On one hand, assessing the accuracy of this low-dimensional model (amongst the many) of the tropical atmosphere that take advantage of equatorial long-wave theory [7, 10, 11] is an important ongoing task [12, 13, 14]; on the other hand, different from some test models without instability nor positive Lyapunov exponents [15], this simplified quasi-equilibrium tropical model (2) is more realistic achieved by allowing active barotropic dynamics and coupled nonlinear advection which allows for tropical-extratropical wave interactions [7, 16, 6, 15, 17].

[6, 18] also explore solitary structures (which are not rare in atmospheric science) within these amplitude equations (2) which may explain transfer of energy between waves. The nonlinearly coupled KdV equations

ut−(1−γ)​ux​x​x+u​ux=γ​vx​x​x+(u​v)x2,\displaystyle u_{t}-(1-\gamma)u_{xxx}+uu_{x}=\gamma v_{xxx}+\frac{\left(uv\right)_{x}}{2},
vt−(1−γ)​vx​x​x+v​vx=γ​ux​x​x+(u​v)x2.\displaystyle v_{t}-(1-\gamma)v_{xxx}+vv_{x}=\gamma u_{xxx}+\frac{\left(uv\right)_{x}}{2}.

are actually recast by a linear transformation from these amplitude equations (2) [18]. u,vu,v govern the amplitude of two types of modes, each of which consists of a coupled tropical/midlatitude flow. We choose to work with γ=0\gamma=0

ut−ux​x​x+u​ux=(u​v)x2,\displaystyle u_{t}-u_{xxx}+uu_{x}=\frac{\left(uv\right)_{x}}{2},
vt−vx​x​x+v​vx=(u​v)x2.\displaystyle v_{t}-v_{xxx}+vv_{x}=\frac{\left(uv\right)_{x}}{2}. (3)

due to the generic nature of the interaction [18].

Despite the need to understand its role in atmospheric background [19, 20, 15, 21], analysis of solitons’ behavior is very incomplete and it is precisely at the point of solitary waves that interesting dynamics arise [6]. Notice u≡0u\equiv 0 or v≡0v\equiv 0 are invariant subspaces of (3) with the non-zeron function evolving according to the KdV equation [18]; take v≡0v\equiv 0 as an example, KdV solution includes

u⁡(x,t)=ϵ−2​K​(ϵ−1​(x−c​ϵ−2​t)),K⁡(ξ)=−12​{sech }2​ξ,c=−4.u(x,t)=\epsilon^{-2}K\left(\epsilon^{-1}\left(x-c\epsilon^{-2}t\right)\right),\qquad K(\xi)=-12\sech^{2}\xi,\qquad c=-4.

and c​ϵ−2c\epsilon^{-2} is the traveling velocity of the soliton. Inspired by these solitary structures, Biello [18] presents numerical results showing the collision of one uu-soliton with one vv-soliton initialized by

u⁡(x,0)=K⁡(x),v⁡(x,0)=ϵ−2​K​(ϵ−1​(x−xv0)),u(x,0)=K(x),\qquad v(x,0)=\epsilon^{-2}K\left(\epsilon^{-1}\left(x-x^{0}_{v}\right)\right), (4)

but only with relatively large ϵ=0.75\epsilon=0.75. Indeed, two solitons remain their solitary form before they come close to each other and interaction happens later on even though such initialization is well-posed due to work [22, 23, 24]. Just by numerical simulation majorly with ϵ=0.75\epsilon=0.75, Biello [18] is sharp enough to insinuate some details of the interaction including shears, a small amount of rightward traveling radiation generated, etc., and a broad range of interesting and unexplained of behavior is displayed in just few numerical examples [18]. As a typical phenomenon in the simulation, the transversely narrow and sharply peaked soliton shape results in an eye-catching but small scale centrosymmetric precursor radiation in vv. Such a peak has been observed experimentally in figure 6 and provides a possible mechanism for the formation of shear and radiation show in figure 4,6; [18] also presents analogous shear, peak, radiation.

1.2 Multiple-scale model and approximation results

In this paper, we focus on the case of ϵ→0\epsilon\to 0 in (4). Notably, numerical simulation of solitary interaction is both our start and our end for solitons’ behavior studying. Speaking of simulations, radiations during and after interaction of solitons pose a particular difficulty for theoretical investigation and numerical simulations of solitary waves representing ”soliton amplitudes”. Eventually, we successfully apply multiple-scale model to analytically predict radiations, interaction (with ϵ→0\epsilon\to 0):

  1. 1.

    the ansatz of multiple scale model is

    u⁡(x,ϵ−1​x,ϵ−3​t)=\displaystyle u(x,\epsilon^{-1}x,\epsilon^{-3}t)= U0​(x)+UF​(x,ϵ−1​x,ϵ−3​t)\displaystyle U^{0}(x)+U^{F}(x,\epsilon^{-1}x,\epsilon^{-3}t)
    +ϵ​UB​(x,ϵ−1​x,ϵ−3​t)+o⁡(ϵ),\displaystyle+\epsilon U^{B}(x,\epsilon^{-1}x,\epsilon^{-3}t)+o(\epsilon),
    v⁡(x,ϵ−1​x,ϵ−3​t)=\displaystyle v(x,\epsilon^{-1}x,\epsilon^{-3}t)= ϵ−2​V0​(ϵ−1​x,ϵ−3​t)+VF​(x,ϵ−1​x,ϵ−3​t)\displaystyle\epsilon^{-2}V^{0}(\epsilon^{-1}x,\epsilon^{-3}t)+V^{F}(x,\epsilon^{-1}x,\epsilon^{-3}t)
    +ϵ​VR​(x,ϵ−1​x,ϵ−3​t)+o⁡(ϵ);\displaystyle+\epsilon V^{R}(x,\epsilon^{-1}x,\epsilon^{-3}t)+o(\epsilon);

    where we have two scales in space and a single scale in time; or alternatively

    u⁡(x,X,T)\displaystyle u(x,X,T) =U0​(x)+UF​(x,X,T)+ϵ​UB​(x,X,T)+o⁡(ϵ),\displaystyle=U^{0}(x)+U^{F}(x,X,T)+\epsilon U^{B}(x,X,T)+o(\epsilon),
    v⁡(x,X,T)\displaystyle v(x,X,T) =ϵ−2​V0​(X,T)+VF​(x,X,T)+ϵ​VR​(x,X,T)+o⁡(ϵ).\displaystyle=\epsilon^{-2}V^{0}(X,T)+V^{F}(x,X,T)+\epsilon V^{R}(x,X,T)+o(\epsilon). (5)

    where small space scale is X=ϵ−1​xX=\epsilon^{-1}x and the single time scale is T=ϵ−3​tT=\epsilon^{-3}t (fast time).

    U0U^{0} is the base of wave uu and V0V^{0} is approximately the original sharp soliton of wave vv. UFU^{F} (figure 1) is fleeting solitary structure inside wave uu while (inconspicuous) VFV^{F} is the counterpart for wave vv. ϵ​VR\epsilon V^{R} is precursor vv radiation (figure 2, 6), one of our focuses of attention while (less important and obscure as well) ϵ​UB\epsilon U^{B} is the bruise left on uu after the interaction.

  2. 2.

    the model captures mechanism (three phases of interaction) for the formation of shear and radiation:

    precursor vv-radiation is formed firstly; then it interacts with uu, forming uu-radiation and vv-radiation in-situ.

  3. 3.

    the precursor vv radiation (after the interaction) is of the form

    ϵ​VR​(x,X,T)=ϵ​CVR​R​(x), as ​T→∞,\epsilon V^{R}(x,X,T)=\epsilon C^{R}_{V}R(x),\mbox{ as }T\to\infty, (6)

    where normalized R⁡(x)=3​32​sinh⁡(x)​cosh3⁡(x)R(x)=\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}\sinh(x)\cosh^{3}(x) and CVRC^{R}_{V} is a positive constant representing height of VRV^{R}: CVR=1.03∼1.14C^{R}_{V}=1.03\sim 1.14 from simulation (figure 2,6,7; table 2) and our WKB model predicts CVR=4.11C^{R}_{V}=4.11 (second part of figure 10; table 2; derivation in (9jkoy)). By comparison, our WKB model’s prediction of less important UBU^{B} agrees extremely well with numerical simulations with CUB=−15.37C^{B}_{U}=-15.37 (figure 4,8, first part of figure 10; table 1; derivation in (9jkox)) within ϵ​UB​(x,X,T)=ϵ​CUB​R​(x)\epsilon U^{B}(x,X,T)=\epsilon C^{B}_{U}R(x), as T→∞T\to\infty.

1.3 Outline of solution strategy

The objective of this work is to use multiple scale model to predict ”precursor” radiation ϵ​VR\epsilon V^{R} (figure 2,6) as ϵ→0\epsilon\to 0 in (3,4). Our analytical strategy has a few key steps which exploit the multi-scale structure observed from numerical simulations. Our steps will proceed as follows:

  1. 1.

    We present in section 1.4 numerical simulations to better describe the interaction we are to analyse. Simulations also motivate two important tools for asymptotic analysis – multiple scale ansatz and fast-slow decomposition.

  2. 2.

    Motivated by simulations, we present in section 2.1 our multiple scale model to predict ϵ​VR\epsilon V^{R}, ”precursor” radiation of vv. Connections to its numerical motivations (section 1.4) are indispensably focused.

  3. 3.

    Also motivated by simulations, we mathematically clarify in section 2.2 the fast-slow decomposition. Connections to their numerical motivations (section 1.4) are indispensably focused . This allows us to solve equations arisen in WKB theory by reducing PDEs to ODEs.

  4. 4.

    Equipped with the multiple-scale model and fast-slow decomposition, we are able, in section 2.3, to predict the simple analytic solution for the ”precursor” vv-radiation ϵ​VR\epsilon V^{R} and explain the mechanism of interaction. It is convenient to transform equations into moving frame in this section.

1.4 Numerical simulation with ϵ=10−2\epsilon=10^{-2}

As for ansatz (5), V0​(X,T)=K⁡(X−c​T)V^{0}(X,T)=K(X-cT) is approximately the original sharp soliton of wave vv; correspondingly, U0U^{0} is the base of wave uu, approximately U0=K⁡(x)U^{0}=K(x) since

K⁡(x−c​ϵ3​T)=K⁡(x)−c​ϵ3​Kx​(x)​T=K⁡(x)+O⁡(ϵ3).K(x-c\epsilon^{3}T)=K(x)-c\epsilon^{3}K_{x}(x)T=K(x)+O(\epsilon^{3}).

At first glimpse, fleeting solitary structure

UF​(x,X,T)=u⁡(x,X,T)−U0​(x)+o⁡(ϵ0)=u⁡(x,X,T)−K⁡(x)+o⁡(ϵ0)U^{F}(x,X,T)=u(x,X,T)-U^{0}(x)+o(\epsilon^{0})=u(x,X,T)-K(x)+o(\epsilon^{0}) (7)

is very eye-catching in figure 1; after a zoom-in, slow–moving ”precursor” radiation ϵ​VR\epsilon V^{R} (figure 2,6) is a more intriguing feature. Although less eye-catching, observations of UFU^{F} (figure 3) is naturally presented later on. Afterwards, UBU^{B} (figure 4) is more obscure (overshadowed by U0U^{0}) but validate our multiple scale model while establishing our model. Lastly, observations of VFV^{F} is difficult and actually do not play a major role while establishing our model but help us validate our model.

Under this philosophy, we next orderly present observation of UF,VR,UBU^{F},V^{R},U^{B} in this section (section 1.4).

2 Asymptotic approximation of the coupled KdV

We will first perform all of numerical simulations in the case with ϵ=10−2\epsilon=10^{-2}. The essence of simulation is captured by this example, which can easily be generalized to the case with ϵ→0\epsilon\to 0.

These simulations also validate multiple-scale ansatz (5) and the fast-slow decomposition (9ja, 9jb, 9jc, 9jd) in case of ϵ→0\epsilon\to 0.

2.1 Multiple scale model: ansatz and equations

After concluding ansatz (5) from numerical simulations of (3), we substitute the ansatz (5) as well as ∂∂x→ϵ−1​∂∂X+∂∂x\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\to\epsilon^{-1}\frac{\partial}{\partial X}+\frac{\partial}{\partial x}, ∂∂t→ϵ−3​∂∂T\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\to\epsilon^{-3}\frac{\partial}{\partial T} into Biello’s equations (3) and get (3) with respect to different order of ϵ\epsilon as:

ϵ−5​𝒦​(V0)+ϵ−3​[ℒ⁡(VF)+(V0​VF)X]\displaystyle\epsilon^{-5}{\cal K}(V^{0})+\epsilon^{-3}\left[{\cal L}\left(V^{F}\right)+(V^{0}V^{F})_{X}\right]
+ϵ−2​[ℒ⁡(VR)+V0​VxF+(VR​V0)X−3​Vx​X​XF]\displaystyle+\epsilon^{-2}[{\cal L}(V^{R})+V^{0}V^{F}_{x}+(V^{R}V^{0})_{X}-3V^{F}_{xXX}]

where

ℒ⁡(f)=fT−fX​X​X,𝒦⁡(f)=ℒ⁡(f)+f​fX.{\cal L}(f)=f_{T}-f_{XXX},\qquad{\cal K}(f)={\cal L}(f)+ff_{X}.

From (9b), we can notice that UF,VF,UBU^{F},V^{F},U^{B} are indispensable for solving the equation for VRV^{R} although ”precursor” radiation VRV^{R} is our focus of attention in the simulation.

2.2 Fast-slow decomposition

Fast-slow decomposition basically means we decompose functions with respect to two pairs of time-length scales – a small length scale XX with fast time TT, and a large length scale xx. At first glimpse, fast-slow decomposition just seems to be an outcome of multiple scale analysis. However, the decomposition is particularly listed since

  1. 1.

    together with ”Heaviside-like” structures HU,HVH^{U},H^{V}, it plays a crucial role to validate the ansatz;

  2. 2.

    it plays an important role in reducing PDEs for UF,VF,UB,VRU^{F},V^{F},U^{B},V^{R} into ODEs (9jkoq, 9jkos, 9jkou, 9jkow) in section 2.3.

Notice that in the stationary frame of reference, the V0V^{0} soliton does not depend on τ\tau. The equation (9jkoa) for UFU^{F} comes endowed with boundary values UF​(x,ξ,τ)→0U^{F}(x,\xi,\tau)\to 0 as ξ→±∞\xi\to\pm\infty and initial condition UF​(x,ξ,T)→0U^{F}(x,\xi,T)\to 0 as τ→−∞\tau\rightarrow-\infty.

Eventually, the decomposition turn to be:

UF​(x,X,T)={sech }2⁡(x)​SU​(X−c​T),U^{F}(x,X,T)=\sech^{2}(x)S^{U}(X-cT), (9ja)
VF​(x,X,T)={sech }2⁡(x)​SV​(X−c​T),V^{F}(x,X,T)=\sech^{2}(x)S^{V}(X-cT), (9jb)
UB​(x,X,T)=R⁡(x)​HU​(X−c​T),U^{B}(x,X,T)=R(x)H^{U}(X-cT), (9jc)
VR​(x,X,T)=R⁡(x)​HV​(X−c​T).V^{R}(x,X,T)=R(x)H^{V}(X-cT). (9jd)

or for short:

UF​(x,ξ,τ)={sech }2⁡(x)​SU​(ξ),\displaystyle U^{F}(x,\xi,\tau)=\sech^{2}(x)S^{U}(\xi), VF​(x,ξ,τ)={sech }2⁡(x)​SV​(ξ),\displaystyle\qquad V^{F}(x,\xi,\tau)=\sech^{2}(x)S^{V}(\xi),
UB​(x,ξ,τ)=R⁡(x)​HU​(ξ),\displaystyle U^{B}(x,\xi,\tau)=R(x)H^{U}(\xi), VR​(x,ξ,τ)=R⁡(x)​HV​(ξ),\displaystyle\qquad V^{R}(x,\xi,\tau)=R(x)H^{V}(\xi),

since U0U_{0} component of wave uu almost unmoved with respect to wave vv. Here moving frame ξ=X−c​T\xi=X-cT is presented in advance and will be utilized as a customized frame while reducing PDEs into ODEs in section 2.3.

2.3 Solving for Biello’s equation in moving frame

Substituting ansatz (5) into (3), Biello’s equations become (9a, 9b), which can be written out versus different order of ϵ\epsilon as:

ℒ⁡(UF)−[V0​UF]X2≡U0​V0,X2,{\cal L}(U^{F})-\frac{\left[V^{0}U^{F}\right]_{X}}{2}\equiv\frac{U_{0}V_{0,X}}{2}, (9jka)
ℒ⁡(VF)+[V0​VF]X≡[UF​V0]X+U0​V0,X2,{\cal L}(V^{F})+\left[V^{0}V^{F}\right]_{X}\equiv\frac{\left[U^{F}V^{0}\right]_{X}+U_{0}V_{0,X}}{2},\textbf{} (9jkb)
ℒ⁡(UB)−[V0​UB]X≡[U0,x+UxF]​V0+3​Ux​X​XF,{\cal L}(U^{B})-\left[V^{0}U^{B}\right]_{X}\equiv\left[U_{0,x}+U^{F}_{x}\right]V^{0}+3U^{F}_{xXX}, (9jkc)
ℒ⁡(VR)+[V0​VR]X≡[V0​UB]X+[U0,x+UxF]​V0−V0​VxF+3​Vx​X​XF.{\cal L}(V^{R})+\left[V^{0}V^{R}\right]_{X}\equiv\left[V^{0}U^{B}\right]_{X}+\left[U_{0,x}+U^{F}_{x}\right]V^{0}-V^{0}V^{F}_{x}+3V^{F}_{xXX}. (9jkd)

where

ℒ⁡(f)=fT−fX​X​X,U0=K⁡(x),V0=K⁡(X−c​T).{\cal L}(f)=f_{T}-f_{XXX},\qquad U_{0}=K(x),\qquad V^{0}=K(X-cT). (9jkl)

These equations have simple structures, three aspects of which are very illuminating:

  1. 1.

    They each have an in-homogeneity listed, separately, on right hand sides of each equation for UF,VF,UB,VRU^{F},V^{F},U^{B},V^{R}.

  2. 2.

    The first order TT-derivatives and the third order XX-derivatives are endowed by linear KdV operator LL.

  3. 3.

    The in-homogeneous terms for VF,UBV^{F},U^{B} only involves UFU^{F}; the one for VRV^{R} involves UF,VFU^{F},V^{F}. Therefore, we can solve equations VF,UBV^{F},U^{B} after solving UFU^{F} and eventually solve VRV^{R}.

2.3.1 Perspectives in moving frame

In the limit that ϵ→0\epsilon\to 0, it is tantamount to viewing equations in moving frame ξ⁡(X,T)≡X−c​T\xi(X,T)\equiv X-cT, τ⁡(X,T)≡T\tau(X,T)\equiv T which is naturally inspired by numerical simulations by referring to figure 3, 4, 6 for UF,UB,VRU^{F},U^{B},V^{R} and correspondingly, figure 5, 8, 7 for SU,HU,HVS^{U},H^{U},H^{V}. Chain rule implies

[∂∂X,∂∂T]\displaystyle\left[\frac{\partial}{\partial X},\frac{\partial}{\partial T}\right] ≡[∂∂ξ,∂∂τ]​[∂ξ∂X​(X,T)∂ξ∂T​(X,T)∂τ∂X​(X,T)∂τ∂T​(X,T)]≡[∂∂ξ,∂∂τ]​[1401]\displaystyle\equiv\left[\frac{\partial}{\partial\xi},\frac{\partial}{\partial\tau}\right]\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}\frac{\partial\xi}{\partial X}(X,T)&　\frac{\partial\xi}{\partial T}(X,T)\\ \frac{\partial\tau}{\partial X}(X,T)&　\frac{\partial\tau}{\partial T}(X,T)\end{array}\right]\equiv\left[\frac{\partial}{\partial\xi},\frac{\partial}{\partial\tau}\right]\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}1&　4\\ 0&1\end{array}\right]
⇔\displaystyle\Leftrightarrow ∂∂X≡∂∂τ−c​∂∂ξ,∂∂T≡∂∂τ,\displaystyle\frac{\partial}{\partial X}\equiv\frac{\partial}{\partial\tau}-c\frac{\partial}{\partial\xi},\qquad\frac{\partial}{\partial T}\equiv\frac{\partial}{\partial\tau},

or for short,

ξ⁡(X,T)≡X−c​T,τ⁡(X,T)≡T\displaystyle\xi(X,T)\equiv X-cT,\qquad\tau(X,T)\equiv T
⇒\displaystyle\Rightarrow ∂∂X≡∂∂τ−c​∂∂ξ,∂∂T≡∂∂τ.\displaystyle\frac{\partial}{\partial X}\equiv\frac{\partial}{\partial\tau}-c\frac{\partial}{\partial\xi},\qquad\frac{\partial}{\partial T}\equiv\frac{\partial}{\partial\tau}. (9jkn)

Performing the changing of variables on equations (9jka,9jkb,9jkc,9jkd) and substituting U0≡K⁡(x),V0≡K⁡(ξ)U_{0}\equiv K(x),V^{0}\equiv K(\xi) by (9jkl) incidentally. We find (9jka) for UFU^{F} is a linear, in-homogeneous PDE independent of VF,UB,VRV^{F},U^{B},V^{R},

ℒ⁡(UF)−[K⁡(ξ)​UF]ξ2≡K⁡(x)​K​(ξ)ξ2,{\cal L}(U^{F})-\frac{\left[K(\xi)U^{F}\right]_{\xi}}{2}\equiv\frac{K(x)K(\xi)_{\xi}}{2}, (9jkoa)
where linear KdV operator turns into ℒ⁡(f)≡fτ−c​fξ−fξ​ξ​ξ.{\cal L}(f)\equiv f_{\tau}-cf_{\xi}-f_{\xi\xi\xi}. by chain rule (9jkn).

(9jkb,9jkc) for VF,UBV^{F},U^{B} are also linear, each with an in-homogeneity which depends on UFU^{F},

ℒ⁡(VF)+[K⁡(ξ)​VF]ξ≡K⁡(x)​UξF+K⁡(x)​K​(ξ)ξ2,{\cal L}(V^{F})+\left[K(\xi)V^{F}\right]_{\xi}\equiv\frac{K(x)U^{F}_{\xi}+K(x)K(\xi)_{\xi}}{2}, (9jkob)
ℒ⁡(UB)−[K⁡(ξ)​UB]ξ≡[Fx​(x)+UxF]​K​(ξ)+3​Ux​ξ​ξF.{\cal L}(U^{B})-\left[K(\xi)U^{B}\right]_{\xi}\equiv\left[F_{x}(x)+U^{F}_{x}\right]K(\xi)+3U^{F}_{x\xi\xi}. (9jkoc)

Finally, (9jkd) for VRV^{R} is also linear, with an in-homogeneity which depends on UF,VF,UBU^{F},V^{F},U^{B},

ℒ⁡(VR)+[K⁡(ξ)​VR]ξ\displaystyle{\cal L}(V^{R})+\left[K(\xi)V^{R}\right]_{\xi}
≡\displaystyle\equiv [K⁡(ξ)​UB]ξ+[Fx​(x)+UxF]​K​(ξ)−K⁡(ξ)​VxF+3​Vx​ξ​ξF.\displaystyle\left[K(\xi)U^{B}\right]_{\xi}+\left[F_{x}(x)+U^{F}_{x}\right]K(\xi)-K(\xi)V^{F}_{x}+3V^{F}_{x\xi\xi}. (9jkod)

Under this philosophy, in order to predict VRV^{R}, we need to first orderly predict UFU^{F}, VFV^{F}, UBU^{B}. Later in this section (section 2.3), we will predict them in order of UFU^{F}, VFV^{F}, UB,VRU^{B},V^{R}.

2.3.2 Solution of UFU^{F}

From fast-slow decomposition, we know that (9jkoa) has an exact solution in the form:

UF​(x,ξ,τ)={sech }2⁡(x)​SU​(ξ),U^{F}(x,\xi,\tau)=\sech^{2}(x)S^{U}(\xi), (9jkop)

where we actually seek the solution for UFU^{F} independent of τ\tau.

Substituting (9jkop) into (9jkoa) we find the ODE for GG:

Sξ​ξU−[4+6​{sech }2⁡(ξ)]​SU=−72​{sech }2⁡(ξ).S^{U}_{\xi\xi}-\left[4+6\sech^{2}(\xi)\right]S^{U}=-72\sech^{2}(\xi). (9jkoq)

2.3.3 Solution of VFV^{F}

Again according to fast-slow decomposition, we seek a solution of the form:

VF​(x,ξ,τ)={sech }2⁡(x)​SV​(ξ),V^{F}(x,\xi,\tau)=\sech^{2}(x)S^{V}(\xi), (9jkor)

After substituting (9jkop ,9jkor) into equation (9jkob), we find the ODE for SV​(ξ)S^{V}(\xi)

Sξ​ξV−[4−12​{sech }2⁡(ξ)]​SV=6​[SU​(ξ)−12]​{sech }2⁡(ξ).S^{V}_{\xi\xi}-[4-12\sech^{2}(\xi)]S^{V}=6[S^{U}(\xi)-12]\sech^{2}(\xi). (9jkos)

with boundary values limξ→−∞SV​(ξ)=limξ→∞SV​(ξ)=0{\displaystyle}\lim_{\xi\to-\infty}S^{V}(\xi)=\lim_{\xi\to\infty}S^{V}(\xi)=0 according to figure 5 of numerical simulation. Figure 11 (second) plots SVS^{V} with SV​(−10)=SV​(10)=0S^{V}(-10)=S^{V}(10)=0.

2.3.4 Solution of UBU^{B}

Again according to fast-slow decomposition, we seek a solution of the form:

UB​(x,ξ,τ)=R⁡(x)​HU​(ξ).U^{B}(x,\xi,\tau)=R(x)H^{U}(\xi). (9jkot)

After substituting (9jkop ,9jkor, 9jkot) into equation (9jkoc), we find that the ODE for HU​(ξ)H^{U}(\xi)

Hξ​ξU−[4+6​{sech }2⁡(ξ)]​HU=4​33​[2​∫−∞ξ[12−SU​(η)]​{sech }2⁡(η)​𝑑η+SξU].H^{U}_{\xi\xi}-[4+6\sech^{2}(\xi)]H^{U}=\frac{4\sqrt{3}}{3}\left[2\int_{-\infty}^{\xi}[12-S^{U}(\eta)]\sech^{2}(\eta)d\eta+S^{U}_{\xi}\right]. (9jkou)

with left boundary value limξ→−∞HU​(ξ)=0{\displaystyle}\lim_{\xi\to-\infty}H^{U}(\xi)=0 according to figure 8 from numerical simulation; by taking limξ→∞{\displaystyle}\lim_{\xi\rightarrow\infty} on both sides of (9jkou), right boundary value of appears as HU(10)=−4​39∫ℝSU(η)dη=−15.37H^{U}(10)=-\frac{4\sqrt{3}}{9}\int_{{\mathbb{R}}}S^{U}(\eta)d\eta=-15.37 (see C for detail). To conclude, figure 10 (first) shows Heaviside-like HUH^{U}.

2.3.5 Solution of VRV^{R}

Finally, we seek a solution of the form for ”precursor” radiation VRV^{R}:

VR​(x,ξ,τ)=R⁡(x)​HV​(ξ).V^{R}(x,\xi,\tau)=R(x)H^{V}(\xi). (9jkov)

After substituting (9jkop, 9jkor, 9jkot, 9jkov) into equation (9jkod), we find that the terms give an equation for HV​(ξ)H^{V}(\xi)

Hξ​ξV−[4−12{sech }2(ξ)]HV=4​33⋅\displaystyle H^{V}_{\xi\xi}-[4-12\sech^{2}(\xi)]H^{V}=\frac{4\sqrt{3}}{3}\cdot
[HU​(ξ)​{sech }2⁡(ξ)+SξV+2​∫−∞ξ[12−SU​(η)+2​SV​(η)]​{sech }2⁡(η)​𝑑η].\displaystyle\left[H^{U}(\xi)\sech^{2}(\xi)+S^{V}_{\xi}+2\int_{-\infty}^{\xi}\left[12-S^{U}(\eta)+2S^{V}(\eta)\right]\sech^{2}(\eta)d\eta\right]. (9jkow)

with left boundary value limξ→−∞HV​(ξ)=0{\displaystyle}\lim_{\xi\to-\infty}H^{V}(\xi)=0 according to figure 7 from numerical simulation; by taking limξ→∞{\displaystyle}\lim_{\xi\rightarrow\infty} on both sides of (9jkow), right boundary value appears as HV(10)=−4​39∫ℝSV(η)dη≃4.11H^{V}(10)=-\frac{4\sqrt{3}}{9}\int_{{\mathbb{R}}}S^{V}(\eta)d\eta\simeq 4.11 (see C for detail). To conclude, figure 10 (second) shows Heaviside-like HVH^{V}.

2.4 Conclusion of solutions

With our multiple-scale model, we can predict UF,VF,UB,VRU^{F},V^{F},U^{B},V^{R} in ansatz (5). Details of analytic solution utilizes fast-slow decomposition (9ja, 9jb, 9jc, 9jd) and solve fast-moving part of them via ODEs for SU,SV,HU,HVS^{U},S^{V},H^{U},H^{V}.

As a special case, ϵ​VR\epsilon V^{R}, the energy exchange and this subtle ”precursor” radiation can be analytically predicted. Our multiple scale model predicts (6):

ϵ​VR=ϵ​CVR​R​(x),\epsilon V^{R}=\epsilon C^{R}_{V}R(x),

as T→∞T\to\infty where CVR=limξ→∞HV​(ξ)=4.11C^{R}_{V}=\lim_{\xi\to\infty}H^{V}(\xi)=4.11.

Comparisons between model predictions and numerical simulation (with various ϵ\epsilon) are summarized in section 3.

3 Comparison to Numerical Simulations

We compare our model predictions to numerical simulations of the Biello’s equation (3). The system is solved in a doubly periodic domain using a pseudo–spectral method. These simulations were performed with △​x=25N\triangle x=\frac{25}{N} for N=215N=2^{15}, with ϵ=0.1,0.025,0.02,0.014,0.01\epsilon=0.1,0.025,0.02,0.014,0.01, where △​t(△​x)3≃1\frac{\triangle t}{(\triangle x)^{3}}\simeq 1. All solutions were monitored for conservation of energy, Hamiltonian and (two) mean fields to a relative accuracy of at least 10−​1010^{−10}. The last nonlinear energy-conserved term is also an important feature in wave turbulence [25]. Interestingly [26] points out our Biello-Majda system has only these four conserved quantities.

In table 1, we show comparison of max⁡UF\max U^{F} and second local extrema of UBU^{B} between predicted values numerical simulations. We see excellent agreement for UFU^{F}, UBU^{B} between the model predictions and the numerical solutions.

3.1 Comparison of SU,HU,HVS^{U},H^{U},H^{V}

It is not just maximum of UFU^{F}, minimum of VFV^{F}, second local extrema of UBU^{B}, VRV^{R} where we see good agreement between theory and simulation.

Due to fast-slow decomposition, instead of comparing UF,VF,UB,VRU^{F},V^{F},U^{B},V^{R}, we compare solitary SU,SVS^{U},S^{V}, Heaviside-like HU,HVH^{U},H^{V} for the sake of convenience. This is not only because SU,SV,HU,HVS^{U},S^{V},H^{U},H^{V} can be viewed in moving frame ξ=X−c​T\xi=X-cT, but SU,SV,HU,HVS^{U},S^{V},H^{U},H^{V} have much simpler structures as well - solitary SU,SVS^{U},S^{V} and Heaviside-like HU,HVH^{U},H^{V}.

Figure 9 shows SUS^{U}

  • •

    predicted by asymptotic model from (9jkoq) numerically via finite difference method with boundary condition limξ→±∞SU=0\lim_{\xi\to\pm\infty}S^{U}=0 and

  • •

    the ones from simulations plotted via UF​(x,X,T)/{sech }2⁡(x)U^{F}(x,X,T)/\sech^{2}(x) in section 1.4.1 (same philosophy as figure 5).

The solitary structure is evident and our asymptotic model precisely predict solitary UFU^{F} since two plots overlap each other.

Figure 10 (first) shows Heaviside-like HUH^{U} predicted by asymptotic model from (9jkou) numerically via finite difference method with boundary condition limξ→−∞HU=0\lim_{\xi\to-\infty}H^{U}=0 and limξ→−∞HU=−15.37\lim_{\xi\to-\infty}H^{U}=-15.37. This is in excellent agreement with simulation result in figure 4,8 and therefore predict the exact size of UBU^{B}.

Finally, figure 10 (right) shows Heaviside-like HVH^{V} predicted by asymptotic model from (9jkow) numerically via finite difference method with boundary condition limξ→−∞HV=0\lim_{\xi\to-\infty}H^{V}=0 and limξ→∞HV≃4.11\lim_{\xi\to\infty}H^{V}\simeq 4.11. Although this differs from asymptotic simulation shown in figure 2,6,7, it is in agreement with the sign and relative size of VR,HVV^{R},H^{V}. Table 2 concludes the difference.

3.2 Observation and verification of VF,SVV^{F},S^{V}

Numerical observation of VFV^{F} is quite difficult once realizing ϵ−2​V0\epsilon^{-2}V^{0} part of wave vv is very sharp. On the other hand,we can validate our model by validating corresponding fast-slow decomposition (9jb).

However, exact sizes of VF,SVV^{F},S^{V} are inconsistent between the model prediction and simulations. According to (9jkoy), it is precisely integral of SVS^{V} that determines right boundary value for HVH^{V}, which is the important feature for HVH^{V}.

Details of this solitary structure SVS^{V} (figure 11) with two small bumps at two sides is shown in app:observation of H.

4 Conclusion

4.1 Theoretical contribution

Our multiple scale model

  1. 1.

    predict mechanism of interaction within this nonlinearly coupled KdV equations:

    precursor vv-radiation is formed firstly; then it interacts with uu, forming uu-radiation and vv-radiation in-situ.

  2. 2.

    predict with an analytic, asymptotic approximation, the ”precursor” radiation generated during interaction of solitary waves in Biello’s system.

Our establishment of model, motivated by actual numerical simulations, can be applied to different situations, with different models.

4.2 Back to atmospheric background

This solution also gives an essential theoretical piece of the physical explanation for the behavior of radiation in Biello’s system that may lead to a deeper understanding of solitary interaction within the system.

In atmosphere-ocean community, our work can be thought as asymptotic analysis of the nonlinear traveling waves [27, 19, 28] as soliton-like solutions leave behind small scale features after interaction. Furthermore, implications of these structures and interactions for atmospheric tropical/midlatitude behavior is necessary [18]. This sort of nonlinear interaction involving equatorial baroclinic and barotropic Rossby modes might be related to diurnal variations of deep convection in the tropics [21].

Back to atmospheric background, our work can be treated as asymptotic analysis of the nonlinear traveling waves [27, 19, 28] as soliton-like solutions leave behind small scale features. Furthermore, much more work is necessary in order to understand the implications of interactions for atmospheric tropical/midlatitude connections [18]. This sort of nonlinear interaction involving equatorial baroclinic and barotropic Rossby modes might be directly related to diurnal variations of deep convection in the tropics [21].

Appendix D Observation and verification of VFV^{F}

Numerical observation of VFV^{F} is quite difficult once realizing ϵ−2​V0\epsilon^{-2}V^{0} part of wave vv is so tall that one could hardly observe its bottom (namely, the area where vv obtains min⁡v\min v); this corresponds to the fact that in the limit of ϵ→0\epsilon\to 0, vv wave tends to be singular. Luckily, we can balance the order of ϵ\epsilon in (3) instead. This reveals VFV^{F} is of order O⁡(ϵ0)O(\epsilon^{0}).

Figure 11 shows

  • •

    (first) SVS^{V} from numerical simulations near x=0x=0 via the numerical method described above and

  • •

    (second) SVS^{V} predicted by asymptotic model from (9jkos) numerically via finite difference method with Cauchy boundary condition SV​(−10)=SV​(10)=0S^{V}(-10)=S^{V}(10)=0.

The solitary structure with two small bumps at two sides is evident and is a shared feature for theoretical results and numerical results. However, the integral quantity as well as other feature for exact size of SVS^{V} is different. According to (9jkoy), it is precisely this integral quantity that determines right boundary value for HVH^{V}, which is an important feature for HVH^{V}. According to (9jkoy), the inconsistency can be view of ill-prediction of integral quantity of SVS^{V} by our asymptotic model.
